n: Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament, written perhaps around 450 BC, after the temple was rebuilt. The people’s early enthusiasm had faded into routine and doubt. The book unfolds as a series of dialogues: God speaks, the people object, and God answers.

f.g: Means “my messenger” — perhaps a name, perhaps a title (see Malachi 3:1).

n: God begins with love: “I have loved you.” But the people ask, “How have You loved us?” As proof, God points to His choice of Jacob over his twin, Esau.
“I hated Esau” is a Hebrew idiom meaning “I chose Jacob rather than Esau” for the covenant role — not personal hatred. Edom, Esau’s nation, had been devastated.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “loved less” or “did not choose,” as in Genesis 29:31 and Luke 14:26.

n: Edom vows to rebuild, but God says He will tear down whatever they build. They will be known as a wicked land under God’s lasting displeasure.

f.w: They shall build, but I will throw down

n: Israel will see this and declare that the Lord is great even beyond Israel’s borders.
God confronts the priests: a son honors his father and a servant his master. If I am your Father and Master, where is My honor? They ask, “How have we despised Your name?”

f.w: if then I be a father

n: They offer defiled food on God’s altar and treat the Lord’s table — the altar — as if it doesn’t matter.

f.g: Unacceptable offerings; “bread” means food in general.

n: They offer blind, lame, and sick animals — rejects nobody else wants. Would your governor accept such a gift? God deserves our best, not our leftovers.

f.w: if ye offer the blind for sacrifice

n: Go ahead and ask God for favor — but with offerings like these, will He accept you?

f.w: this hath been by your means
f.g: You did this — you are responsible.

n: God wishes someone would just shut the temple doors rather than keep lighting useless fires on His altar. He won’t accept their half-hearted offerings.

f.g: Close the temple gates — stop the meaningless worship.

n: Meanwhile, from sunrise to sunset God’s name will be great among the nations, and pure offerings will be given to Him everywhere. Ironically, outsiders may honor God more than His own priests.

f.w: from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same

n: But you profane God’s name by saying His altar and its food are contemptible.
They complain, “What a bore!” and sniff at worship. They bring stolen, lame, and sick animals. Should God accept that?

f.g: Sniffed in contempt; turned up their noses.
Mauled by wild animals — or taken by robbery.

n: Cursed is the cheat who vows a good male animal but sacrifices a blemished one instead. God is a great King, honored even among the nations.
